rationale: I'm adding a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each condition next to the current relative band powers. It comes from a log-log line fit of the Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha range. The exponent is thought to track the balance between neural excitation and inhibition, and it has been reported to differ in depression. Because it is a slope, it doesn't change with amplitude scale, so it should also transfer to the external amplifier. Relative band power mixes this broadband tilt with true oscillatory peaks, so the separate feature should help.

I'm re-referencing every recording to the common average (subtracting the mean across channels at each sample) before the Welch PSD. The original reference mixes its own activity into every channel and smears the topography of relative power. It also differs between clinics: TDBRAIN uses a different montage than Mumtaz's linked ears. Average reference makes the per-channel spectra roughly reference-independent, so they should show local depression-related differences more clearly and transfer better to the external amplifier.

I'm switching the Welch PSD from mean to median averaging across the 2-s segments (`average='median'`). These recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few segments with blinks, movement or muscle bursts can inflate the mean spectrum, especially delta and gamma, and swamp the depression-related changes in relative power. The median works like built-in epoch rejection: it is robust to those outlier segments, needs no thresholds, and doesn't depend on recording length or amplifier, so it should also carry over to the external data.

I'm adding a second model built on spatial covariance in Riemannian tangent space, and averaging its probabilities with the existing relative band-power model. It uses CAR, a 4th-order band-pass into theta, alpha and beta, trace-normalized and shrunk covariances per condition, a tangent space fitted on the training fold only, and L2 logistic regression. Covariance captures inter-regional coupling and spatial patterns in depression that per-channel power can't see. Trace normalization keeps it independent of amplitude scale, and the shrinkage handles the rank lost to CAR.

I'm splitting the five broad bands into seven: delta, theta, low alpha (8–10 Hz), high alpha (10–13 Hz), low beta (13–20 Hz), high beta (20–30 Hz) and gamma. Depression has been linked to opposite shifts in the two alpha sub-bands and to raised fast beta, and the broad alpha and beta bands average those changes together. The features stay scale-invariant relative log powers after average re-referencing, so they should still transfer to the external amplifier.

Switching Welch to median averaging cost 0.085 AUROC (round 3). That suggests the large, rare high-power segments carry diagnostic signal: transient bursts, eye and movement activity, possibly differences in vigilance. I'm keeping the current mean-PSD relative band powers and adding a per-channel, per-band burstiness index, log(mean ÷ median of segment band power). It measures how much of each band's power comes from intermittent bursts versus steady activity. Because it is a ratio, it is unaffected by amplitude scale and recording length, so it should transfer to the external data.

I'm replacing the fixed C=0.1 with an L2 strength chosen per training fold by inner 5-fold grouped CV (AUROC, log-spaced grid). The dev pool is small, with about 190 correlated relative-power features. Every feature-adding round so far has hurt, which points to the main limit being the bias–variance tradeoff rather than missing features, so the regularization strength should be set from the training data instead of hard-coded.

Switching to median Welch averaging cost 0.085 AUROC, which suggests some of the signal is in intermittent high-power activity rather than steady rhythms. A likely source is scalp-muscle (EMG) tension, which is raised in depression and can also reflect medication. I'm adding one high-frequency band (55–95 Hz) to the existing log relative band powers. It skips the 50/100 Hz line noise and is still divided by the 1–45 Hz total, so it stays independent of amplitude scale.

I'm adding the individual alpha peak frequency for each condition, computed from the posterior average re-referenced spectrum (P3/P4/Pz/O1/O2) as both the 7–13 Hz centre of gravity and the argmax. Alpha slowing is linked to depression and to the effects of antidepressants and benzodiazepines, and fixed-band relative power can't capture where the peak sits. This adds only 4 features, so variance stays low, and frequency doesn't change with amplitude scale, reference or recording length.

Every feature so far is per-channel spectral power. This adds functional coupling as a new kind of signal: for each channel and condition, the mean magnitude-squared coherence with all other channels in theta, alpha and beta, computed after average re-referencing. Raised alpha and theta coherence is reported in depression. Coherence is a normalized cross-spectrum, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length. Taking the per-channel average (node strength) keeps it to 114 features instead of 171 channel pairs × 3 bands per condition (513).

I'm adding 19 features per condition: each channel's log total 1–45 Hz power minus that subject's average across channels. Per-channel relative band powers drop how overall power is spread across the scalp, so they can't see the frontal eye and temporal muscle artifact topography or the frontal-vs-posterior power balance. Since subtracting the subject's mean cancels amplitude scale, the new features should still transfer to other amplifiers.

I'm averaging the current L2 logistic regression with a random forest trained on the same features, giving equal weight to the probabilities of each. Every feature-adding round except two has hurt, so the limit looks like model variance and missing non-additive structure, not missing features. Artifact- and EMG-related effects (for example a threshold on high-frequency or frontal power) and medication-driven spectral changes are likely non-linear. A low-variance bagged tree ensemble can capture these interactions, and its errors should differ from the linear model's. The features are unchanged, so they stay amplitude-scale free.

The random forest gave the biggest jump so far (+0.081), which suggests threshold-like, non-additive structure in the spectral and topography features, but on a small n with highly correlated features a single bagged forest still has high variance. This change keeps the logistic regression at half the weight and splits the tree half between the existing random forest and an extremely-randomized-trees model. Its random split thresholds give a smoother, lower-variance decision function and errors that differ from the forest's. The features are unchanged and still amplitude-scale free.

I'm switching the random forest to train on sub-recording views. Each recording is cut into 4 equal chunks per condition, and the forest is trained on those plus the full recording, with every view carrying its subject's label. Test predictions average the forest's probabilities over all of a subject's views. The forest is the high-variance part of the ensemble and needs many samples, so within-subject segments act as natural augmentation. Averaging over segments also fits the round-3 finding that intermittent high-power periods carry signal, and splitting by fraction rather than fixed duration keeps it independent of recording length. The logistic regression is unchanged and still sees only full-recording features.

I'm adding frontal and whole-scalp alpha asymmetry: log(right ÷ left) 8–13 Hz power for each homologous channel pair (Fp1/Fp2, F3/F4, F7/F8, C3/C4, T7/T8, P3/P4, P7/P8, O1/O2) in each condition, after average re-referencing. Asymmetry is a classic depression marker and has not been tried yet. It adds only about 16 features and doesn't depend on amplitude scale. The random forest can't build left–right differences from single-channel splits, so these features give it signal it can't currently get.

I'm adding 19 eyes-closed vs eyes-open alpha reactivity features: for each channel, log(EC 8–13 Hz power ÷ EO 8–13 Hz power) after average re-referencing. Weak alpha blocking is reported in depression, and it is a within-subject ratio, so amplitude scale cancels. The random forest can't build cross-condition differences from single-feature splits, so these give it signal it currently can't reach.

I'm adding per-channel kurtosis of the average-referenced signal, in two versions per condition: one filtered to 1–45 Hz and one to the 55–95 Hz high-frequency/EMG band. Earlier rounds suggest the diagnostic signal sits in rare, high-amplitude transients (median averaging lost 0.085, and the high-frequency band and random forest both helped), and the averaged power spectrum blurs those away. Kurtosis measures how heavy-tailed or bursty the signal is, does not change with amplitude scale, and gives the random forest a feature it can split on directly.

I'm extending the per-channel log kurtosis from the broadband 1–45 Hz and 55–95 Hz signals to each classic band: delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz). Broadband kurtosis helped, and it mixes several sources: blinks and eye movements (frontal delta), drowsiness bursts (theta), the waxing and waning of alpha, and beta/EMG bursts. Splitting by band lets the random forest split on each source separately. The features stay scale-free and independent of recording length.

I'm adding a per-channel Higuchi fractal dimension (kmax=10) of the 1–45 Hz band-passed, average-referenced signal for each condition, which adds 38 features. Depression studies repeatedly report higher fractal dimension, i.e. more irregular EEG. The model has no complexity measure yet, and HFD captures waveform irregularity that is neither spectral power nor tail heaviness. It is unaffected by amplitude scale and fairly stable across recording lengths.

Following Hegerl's vigilance-regulation model, MDD tends to show hyperstable vigilance at rest: the EEG drifts less from alpha toward theta/delta over the recording than in healthy controls. The current features average the whole recording into one number and can't see this, so I'm adding per-condition vigilance-dynamics features. The recording is cut into 8 equal fractions, and for each band I take the channel-averaged log relative power in every fraction, then record its slope over normalized time and its spread across the fractions. That is 24 features, all independent of amplitude scale and recording length.
